If you buy a new car you'll want to take it for a test drive. And if you develop
a theory of electricity you'll want to take if for test drive also. In the last
part of the electricity module we'll apply our newly developed understanding of
electrical interactions to electrical circuits.

The story of electrical circuits began with the invention of the electrochemical
cell by the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta. Volta's cells - consisting of
alternating copper and zinc plates separated by paper soaked in salt water -
were able to produce a steady current for long periods of time. This generation
of electric currents was a monumental breakthrough for modern civilization.

At school you might have built a version of Volta's battery from a lemon, penny
(Cu) and nail (Zn). When the battery's operating, zinc is oxidized, H2 gas is
liberated, these reactions functioning to supply electrons to the zinc and
remove electrons from the copper. In this way these reactions 'fuel' the steady
flow of electric charge through a circuit connected across the zinc / copper
terminals. Battery's are marvels of chemistry and physics that harvest the
electrical energy of molecular bonds; so take a moment to thank Volta the next
time you use your phone.

Let me offer an analogy to the electrochemical battery for supplying electric
currents that we'll call the gravochemical battery for supplying water currents.
The electrochemical battery supplies electrical potential energy by harvesting
energy from chemical bonds. Likewise the gravochemical battery supplies
gravitational potential energy by harvesting energy in chemical bonds. The
electrochemical battery involves nature transporting ions from one terminal of
the battery to the other terminal of the battery in order to accrue the
electrical energy derived from chemical bonds (battery food). The gravochemical
battery involves you transporting water from your first floor kitchen (one
terminal of the gravochemical battery) to your second floor bedroom (other
terminal of the gravochemical battery) to accrue the gravitational energy
derived from chemical bonds (your food). The electrochemical battery can then do
work by supplying the stored electrical energy through the flow of an electric
current between the positive / negative battery terminals. And the gravochemical
battery can do work by supplying the stored energy through the flow of a water
current between its second / first floor terminals. Ultimately, both batteries
do work by 'eating' the food of chemical bonds.

Note in quantifying the electrochemical battery's we use the term 'electromotive
force' (or emf, for short). Sources of emfs are devices that convert
non-electrical energy to electrical energy and thereby do work to move charges
in electrical circuits (that's the meaning of the \`electromotive' in the term
emf). For example, a battery harvests chemical energy, a generator harvests
mechanical energy, and solar cells harvest sunlight, to do work on the charges
in the circuit. Note the word 'force' in electromotive force is rather
misleading as the emf \[equation missing in original\] is the work done W per
electric charge q in energizing the circuit. Although the units of emf are
Joules per Coulomb or Volts, its important to recognize that sources of emfs are
devices that convert other energy forms into electrical energy.

In many cases when analyzing circuits we consider the battery as simply, and
only, a source of emf. In such a 'model' the battery's terminal voltage is
exactly the same if drawing 1.0 micro-Amp, 1.0 milli-Amp, 1.0 Amp, or 1.0
kilo-Amps. Of course, you know this statement is ridiculous - you can't
jump-start an eighteen wheeler with the battery from your smoke alarm. In
reality, however, the more electric current you draw, the lower terminal voltage
you see. This fact can be modeled as a battery consisting of a fixed emf
\[equation missing in original\] with a series internal resistance r. For an
Energizer AA alkaline battery the internal resistance is roughly 0.1-0.2 Ohms
(it depends on temperature, age, etc).

Close your eyes and imagine a leafy trail alongside a winding mountain stream,
The flow of water in the stream is called a current and can be described by the
kilograms of water per second or the number of molecules per second. The flow
arises from the gravitational force with water flowing from higher to lower
gravitational potential energy. Now imagine the wires connecting components of a
electrical circuit, The flow of electrons in the wire is called a current and
can be described by the Coulombs of charge per second or the number of electrons
per second. The flow arises from the electric force with charge flowing from
higher to lower electrical potential energy. We'll find it's often helpful to
imagine the water flow in mountain streams when studying circuits of batteries,
resistors, switches and wires.

One thing that's confusing about current is the direction of the current.
Imagine a simple circuit with a light bulb that is connected across the
terminals of a battery. By convention the electric current is defined to flow
from the positive battery terminal to the negative battery terminal. This
direction is downhill in terms of potential V and the direction that a positive
charge would travel as repelled from the positive (like) terminal and attracted
to the negative (unlike) terminal. Of course the negative electrons are actually
flowing the opposite. This direction is uphill in potential V and the direction
that a negative electron would travel as repelled from the negative (like)
terminal and attracted to the positive (unlike) terminal. This makes me wish
that scientists had chosen to call an electron the positive charge and the
proton the negative charge. But we - okay, Benjamin Franklin - didn't do that.

In winter I bet you like your home warm and lights on. You probably also
appreciate the dish washer doing the dishes and the washing machine doing the
laundry. It's household electrical circuits of resistors, switches and wires
that distribute the currents and potentials that run your home and keep you
comfortable. And it brain electrical circuits of neurons, synapses and axons
that fire the currents and potentials that run your brain and keep you thinking.

In class we'll examine some circuits involving batteries, resistors and wires
that distribute currents and voltages to circuit components. Imagine these
circuits as prototypes for the circuits in your home and your brain. Don't be
scared of circuits - you've already been building circuits and distributing
currents / voltages when you hung the Christmas lights on your Christmas tree or
charged your Fitbit, phone, laptop, etc., from a power strip. We'll study such
circuits through Ohm's law and Kirchoff's laws, understanding series and
parallel wiring, and exploring the supply, transport and dissipation of energy
and power in circuits.

Ohms law - V = IR - is a relationship between the potential V and the current I
in a conductor. The law is not a fundamental law of nature like F = ma or p =
mv. Ohm's isn't exact, its often very good, its sometimes far off , it
represents an empirical description of some materials (not other materials). It
was of practical importance and bought order to sundry measurements of currents
and voltages through / across materials.

Ohms law is 200 years old and predates any modern understanding that matter is
made of atoms, that atoms are made of electrons and nuclei, and electrical
conductors are certain materials with mobile electrons. It wasn't until 1900
that some sort of microscopic explanation of Ohms law in terms of
negatively-charged electrons flowing through positively-charged ion obstructions
- like the metal balls of a pinball machine - was understood.

A falling rain drop in the atmosphere doesn't accelerate under the gravitational
force because it additionally experiences a drag force from falling through the
air's atoms and consequently 'drifts' at constant velocity from cloud to earth.
A moving electron in a conductor doesn't accelerate under the electrical force
because it also experiences a drag force from moving through the metal's ions
and consequently drifts at constant velocity from negative to positive battery
terminals. This drag or resistance, R, of the metal's ions is why V = I R.
